source_text: Quid, quod istam pulcherrimam famulam tuam, quam me pudet assidue vel vituperando nominare, te autem praedicare non pudet: "Commendatiorem fieri putas, quod ei serviunt, ut ardentius excitetur, etiam ceterae corporis partes, sive oculi videntes ad concupiscendum, sive alia membra in osculis et amplexibus"? Aures quoque hominis quomodo ei subderes invenisti, et erexisti eius vetustissimum quidem, sed plane gloriosissimum titulum, commemorans quod in expositione Consiliorum suorum Tullius posuit: Quia cum vinolenti adolescentes tibiarum etiam cantu, ut fit, instincti, mulieris pudicae fores frangerent; admonuisse tibicinam, ut spondeum caneret, Pythagoras dicitur: quod cum illa fecisset, tarditate modorum et gravitate cantus illorum furentem petulantiam resedisse … consentitur ei potius quam imperatur … aliis concitatur stimulis, vel modulamine frangitur et sedatur
pass_a_gloss: What of this: that this most beautiful handmaid of yours, whom it shames me constantly even in blaming to name, but you it does not shame to praise: 'you think (her) to become more commendable, because there serve her, so that she be more ardently roused, also the other parts of the body, either the eyes seeing for desiring, or other members in kisses and embraces'? The ears also of man, how you might subject (them) to her, you found, and you raised her very old indeed, but plainly most glorious title, mentioning what Tullius set in the exposition of his Counsels: that when drunken youths, stirred also by the song of pipes, as happens, were breaking the doors of a chaste woman, Pythagoras is said to have advised the piper-girl to play a spondee; and when she had done it, by the slowness of the measures and the gravity of the song their raging wantonness subsided. — It is consented to rather than commanded. — It is stirred by other goads, or by melody is broken and calmed.

lemmas.gloss: handmaid, female servant (Augustine's figure for desire)
more commendable, more to be praised

pass_b_english: Augustine reports, speaking to Julian: “What of the fact that this most beautiful handmaid of yours, whom I am ashamed to name so often even to blame her, but whom you are not ashamed to praise, ‘you think becomes more commendable because the other parts of the body also serve her so that she is roused more ardently, whether the eyes, seeing in order to desire, or other members in kisses and embraces’? You also found how to make a man’s ears subject to her, and you raised up her title, very ancient indeed but plainly most glorious, recalling what Tullius set down in the account of his Counsels.”

When drunken young men, excited also by flute music as often happens, were breaking down a chaste woman’s door, Pythagoras is said to have told the flute player to play a solemn spondaic rhythm. When she did, the slowness of the measures and gravity of the song quieted their raging insolence. [Cicero, On His Own Counsels, a lost work.]
It receives consent rather than commands.
It is excited by other stimuli, or broken and quieted by music.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-d): the old English summarised Augustine's report ('Augustine reports that Julian ...') instead of translating it. Now a translation of the Latin clause(s) that carry Julian's words or Augustine's report of them, with Augustine named as speaker where the words are his; nothing added that the Latin does not say. Omitted stretches inside a paragraph are marked with an ellipsis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded. This row is Augustine's report; Pass A glosses only the Julian words recoverable here. This row translates Augustine's report addressed to Julian, with Augustine named as speaker; Julian's words are the quoted parts.
